introduction-oltp-vs-olap.core: OLTP databases run many tiny, concurrent, ACID transactions on live state. OLAP warehouses run huge scans that aggregate history. They need opposite designs, so keep analytics off the production database.

first_principles.problem: Someone runs "average order value by country" on the production Postgres. The scan over hundreds of millions of rows eats I/O and CPU, and checkout slows for real customers. One database can't be great at both jobs.
truths: Transactions touch a few whole rows. Analytics touch a few columns of many rows.
Big scans compete with live traffic for the same resources.
Live state and historical insight have different owners and lifecycles.
derivation: **OLTP** (Postgres, MySQL): row-oriented, fast, concurrent, ACID, GB to low TB.
**OLAP** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift): column-oriented, scan-optimised, TB to PB.
**Golden rule**: never run heavy analytics on production OLTP.
Move data to the warehouse (replicate or export) and analyse there. It's an **architectural boundary**, not just a tuning tip.

analogy.title: Waiters vs. the owner's monthly report
analogy.story: Waiters take orders and process payments: small, fast, constant actions. The owner reviews a month of sales by dish category: one big, slow analysis. If the owner did that analysis at the till during dinner rush, service would stall.
mapping: Analysis at the till during rush
analogy.breaks: The owner can wait until closing time. Analysts need answers during the day, which is why a separate warehouse is the solution, not "run it at night".

example.title: A report that slows checkout
example.scenario: A monthly revenue query runs on the primary at 10 a.m.

steps.label: Impact
steps.detail: The scan evicts hot pages and saturates disk, so checkout queries wait.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Load orders into BigQuery nightly or via CDC, and run the report there.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Production returns to normal and the report runs faster on columnar storage.

example.outcome: each system does the job it was designed for, and neither hurts the other.

points: OLTP = live transactions, OLAP = historical analysis.

check.q: Why is a warehouse also bad at OLTP-style workloads?
check.a: Frequent small updates and deletes are hostile to columnar, bulk-optimised storage. It's built for big reads, not tiny writes.

columnar-storage-the-secret-sauce.core: Warehouses store each column contiguously, so queries read only the columns they use, similar values compress 5–10×, and per-block min/max metadata (zone maps) lets the engine skip whole partitions.

first_principles.problem: `AVG(age)` over 500 M users in a row store reads 200-byte rows to use 4 bytes each, wasting 98% of the I/O. At petabyte scale that's hours and huge bills.
truths: Values in one column are alike and compress well.
Knowing a block's min/max can prove it holds no matches.
derivation: **Store by column**: read only the needed columns (**selective I/O**). 3 of 50 columns means about 6% of the bytes.
**Compress** each column (run-length, dictionary): 5–10× smaller.
Keep **zone maps / sort keys**: min/max per micro-partition, so filters prune blocks without reading them.
Separate **compute from storage** (Snowflake) so many warehouses query the same data without contention.

analogy.title: A spreadsheet printed column by column
analogy.story: Print every column as its own booklet. To average everyone's age you pick up only the "age" booklet. Each booklet has a cover note saying "ages 18–35 inside", so if you want people over 60 you don't even open it.
analogy.breaks: Booklets are equally easy to update. Columnar storage makes single-row updates expensive, because one row's fields live in many places.

example.title: "Why is Snowflake faster than Postgres for analytics?"
example.scenario: The same AVG(age) WHERE age > 60 over 500 M users.

steps.label: Columnar
steps.detail: Read about 1% of the bytes a row store would.

steps.label: Pruning
steps.detail: Micro-partitions whose max(age) < 60 are skipped entirely.

steps.label: Concurrency
steps.detail: Separate virtual warehouses don't fight for I/O.

example.outcome: you can explain warehouse speed in three concrete layers, not "it's in the cloud".

points: Read only the columns you need.

check.a: Data physically ordered or clustered by the filter column, so each block's min/max range is narrow and most blocks can be skipped.

schemas-star-vs-snowflake.core: Analytical models separate facts (measurable events) from dimensions (descriptive context). The star schema keeps dimensions denormalised for simple, fast joins, and the snowflake schema normalises them to save storage that rarely matters.

first_principles.problem: Raw operational tables are awkward for analysis: many joins, cryptic codes, no calendar attributes. Analysts need a predictable shape where every question is "join facts to a few dimensions, filter, aggregate".
truths: Business events (sales, views) are numerous and measurable.
Descriptions (product, store, date) are fewer and change slowly.
In cloud warehouses storage is cheap and joins cost time.
derivation: Put events in a long **fact table**: metrics plus foreign keys.
Put context in **dimension tables**: product, store, date (with quarter, holiday flags…).
**Star**: one hop from fact to each dimension, with region stored right in `dim_stores` (deliberate redundancy).
**Snowflake**: normalise dimensions into hierarchies, which saves negligible space and adds joins and complexity.
Default to **star**, and snowflake only for a real, measured storage problem.

analogy.title: A receipt book and reference cards
analogy.story: Every sale is a line in a huge receipt book (facts): item code, store code, date code, amount. Reference cards explain codes: what item 42 is, where store 7 is. Star: each card has everything on it. Snowflake: the item card says "category: see card C3", so you need another lookup.
analogy.breaks: Paper cards cost money to print, so snowflaking once saved real space. In a cloud warehouse the saved megabytes are rounding error, while the extra joins on billions of fact rows aren't.

example.title: Total sales by category in Q4 2023

steps.label: Star
steps.detail: Category is a column in dim_products, so it's two simple joins.

steps.label: Snowflake
steps.detail: Category lives in dim_categories, so there's an extra join across 10 B fact rows.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: Star: simpler for analysts and faster.

code.text:
SELECT p.category, SUM(f.amount_sold) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_products p ON f.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN dim_dates d    ON f.date_id = d.date_id
WHERE d.year = 2023 AND d.quarter = 4
GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY revenue DESC;

example.outcome: every analytical question follows one simple, fast pattern.

points: Snowflake rarely pays off in the cloud.

check.q: Why is redundancy acceptable in star-schema dimensions?
check.a: Dimension tables are small, storage is cheap, and eliminating joins over huge fact tables is worth far more.

the-pipeline-etl-vs-elt.core: ETL transforms data on a separate server before loading. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse with SQL (dbt). The difference is where compute lives, and cheap, elastic warehouse compute makes ELT the modern default.

first_principles.problem: Data starts in app databases, SaaS APIs and logs, messy and inconsistent. It has to be cleaned and modelled for analysis. Old pipelines did that on a separate ETL server, a bottleneck that also threw away the raw data, so bugs couldn't be fixed by re-running.
truths: Transformation logic will have bugs and will change.
Raw data, once discarded, may be impossible to get back.
Cloud warehouses have elastic compute that's good at SQL.
derivation: **ETL** (pre-cloud): extract, then transform on a separate server, then load clean data. Made sense when warehouse CPU was scarce.
**ELT** (cloud): extract, **load raw** into a staging schema, then transform **in the warehouse** with SQL.
Manage transformations with **dbt**: SQL models, dependencies, tests, docs.
Keep the **raw layer append-only** as an audit trail and replay source.
Exception: mask or anonymise PII **before** load if policy forbids raw PII in the warehouse.

analogy.title: Cooking at home vs. in a big kitchen
analogy.story: ETL: you prep and cook everything at home on a small stove, then bring only the finished dish to the party, and if the recipe was wrong, the raw ingredients are gone. ELT: you bring the raw groceries to a huge professional kitchen, cook there, and keep the groceries, so you can re-cook if the recipe changes.
analogy.breaks: Bringing raw groceries is harmless. Loading raw personal data into a warehouse can breach privacy rules, so sensitive fields may need masking first.

example.title: Fixing a revenue bug retroactively
example.scenario: A transformation double-counted refunds for 6 months.

steps.label: ETL world
steps.detail: Raw data is gone, so you must re-extract 6 months from the source, if you even can.

steps.label: ELT world
steps.detail: Fix `fact_sales.sql` and rebuild from the raw layer.

steps.label: Test
steps.detail: Add a dbt test so it can't regress.

code.text:
models/
  staging/stg_orders.sql      -- clean raw.orders
  marts/fact_sales.sql        -- join + aggregate
$ dbt run --select fact_sales --full-refresh && dbt test

example.outcome: mistakes in logic become a re-run, not a data-loss incident.

points: The real difference is where compute lives.
ELT + dbt is the cloud default.

check.q: When might you still transform before loading?
check.a: When raw data contains PII that policy forbids storing in the warehouse, so it must be masked or anonymised first.

partitioning-and-clustering-query-perfor.core: Partition big tables by a low-cardinality column (usually date) so queries read only matching segments, and cluster or sort within partitions by high-cardinality filter columns so zone maps skip blocks. Don't over-partition.

first_principles.problem: Even columnar scans of a multi-trillion-row fact table are slow, and warehouses charge per byte scanned or per compute second. Reading five years of data to answer a one-day question wastes both.
truths: Physically grouping rows lets the engine skip groups.
Too many tiny partitions make metadata the bottleneck.
derivation: **Partition** by date (daily is common) so a one-day query reads one partition (about 99.95% less).
**Cluster** within partitions by frequent high-cardinality filters (store_id, user_id) so block min/max become narrow.
Combine: **partition by date, cluster by the other filter**.
Avoid **partition explosion**: never partition by user_id. Skip both for tiny tables (< 1 GB).

analogy.title: A filing room by month, folders sorted by customer
analogy.story: Drawers are labelled by month (partitions), and within each drawer folders are sorted by customer (clustering). To find store 42 in January you open one drawer and go straight to the right section. A drawer per customer (100 million drawers) would make the room impossible to navigate.
analogy.breaks: Drawers stay sorted. In warehouses, new data lands unsorted and clustering degrades, so it must be maintained (automatic reclustering costs credits).

example.title: A 5-year events table queried for one day and one store

steps.label: Partition
steps.detail: The date filter reads 1 of 1,825 daily partitions.

steps.label: Cluster
steps.detail: Inside it, only blocks whose store_id range includes 42 are read.

steps.label: Bill
steps.detail: Bytes scanned, and therefore cost, drop by orders of magnitude.

example.outcome: queries cost and take a tiny fraction of a full scan.

check.a: Millions of partitions make metadata listing and planning slower than the queries. Cluster by user_id instead.
